caption_hook: North Carolina holds a megalodon sea, a granite quarry, quartzite gorges and rock over a billion years old.

layers.name: PUNGO RIVER FORMATION
layers.what: Warm, shallow seas covered eastern North Carolina and teemed with life. The phosphate-rich sand and clay they laid down holds shark teeth, whale bones and seabird fossils.
layers.bonus: Megalodon teeth bigger than a hand have come out of the mine near Aurora.

layers.name: CASTLE HAYNE LIMESTONE
layers.what: A warm Eocene sea piled up shells and the skeletons of tiny animals into thick, pale limestone near Wilmington. Quarries dig it for crushed stone and cement.
layers.bonus: Its holes and cracks make the Castle Hayne aquifer one of the state's top water sources.

layers.name: MOUNT AIRY GRANITE
layers.hook: The rock they call The Rock
layers.what: Molten rock cooled slowly deep underground into pale, fine-grained granite. Erosion later bared it at Mount Airy, where a mile-long quarry bills itself the world's largest open-face granite quarry.
layers.bonus: Its stone went into the Wright Brothers National Memorial and the Arlington Memorial Bridge.

layers.name: CHILHOWEE GROUP
layers.what: Sand from ancient beaches and shallow seas was baked and squeezed into very hard quartzite. It resists erosion, so it forms the rugged cliffs and ridges of Linville Gorge.
layers.bonus: Linville Gorge is nicknamed the Grand Canyon of the Southern Appalachians.

layers.name: BLOWING ROCK GNEISS
layers.what: Part of the ancient core of the Blue Ridge, this banded rock was baked and squeezed over a billion years ago, long before the Appalachians existed. It forms the cliffs at Blowing Rock.
layers.bonus: Updrafts at The Blowing Rock cliff can toss light objects back up, as legend says.
